Adah
ā'dä
n. (the name of two women: the first wife of Lamech the Cainite, and a Hittite wife of Esau; both stand in households where marriage was corrupted)
From Hebrew 'Adah, ornament or adornment, from a root meaning to pass on or to deck oneself. The name is beautiful; the two households that bore it are not.

Biblical Definition

Adah is borne by two women, and Scripture places each of them at a point where the creation ordinance of marriage is being broken. The first is the elder of the two wives of Lamech, in the line of Cain: “Lamech took unto him two wives: the name of the one was Adah, and the name of the other Zillah” (Gen 4:19) — the first polygamy recorded in the Bible, appearing in the same short passage as the first boast of vengeance. Adah bore Jabal, “the father of such as dwell in tents, and of such as have cattle” (Gen 4:20), so the Cainite line produces real culture and real invention while producing real violence. The second Adah is a Hittite, one of the wives Esau took out of Canaan: “Adah the daughter of Elon the Hittite” (Gen 36:2), and she bore Eliphaz (Gen 36:4), whose son was Amalek. Isaac and Rebekah had been grieved to the soul by these marriages. Both Adahs therefore sit at the head of a line that will trouble the people of God — and Scripture, which could have omitted them, names them, records their sons, and lets the reader trace what came of households built against the pattern of Genesis 2.

Webster 1828 Definition

Webster (1828) has no article for Adah; in sacred history the name belongs to the first wife of Lamech in the line of Cain, and to a Hittite wife of Esau.

expand to see more

ADAH, n. The name signifies ornament or beauty.

The first of the name was one of the two wives of Lamech, the descendant of Cain.

She bore Jabal, the father of such as dwell in tents and have cattle.

The second was the daughter of Elon the Hittite, and a wife of Esau.

She bore Eliphaz, from whom descended the dukes of Edom, and Amalek.

Key Scripture

Gen 4:19 — "And Lamech took unto him two wives: the name of the one was Adah, and the name of the other Zillah."

Gen 4:20 — "And Adah bare Jabal: he was the father of such as dwell in tents, and of such as have cattle."

Gen 36:2 — "Esau took his wives of the daughters of Canaan; Adah the daughter of Elon the Hittite, and Aholibamah the daughter of Anah the daughter of Zibeon the Hivite;"

Gen 36:4 — "And Adah bare to Esau Eliphaz; and Bashemath bare Reuel;"

Modern Corruption

The Bible's record of polygamy is offered as evidence that Scripture endorses plural marriage, or that marriage is a shifting cultural arrangement rather than a creation ordinance.

expand to see more

That the Bible records polygamy is beyond dispute; that it commends it is nowhere the case. The distinction between narration and approval has to be insisted on, because a great deal of argument depends on blurring it. The first polygamist in Scripture is Lamech, a murderer boasting of his vengeance to the two wives he had taken (Gen 4:23) — the account is a description of the corruption of Cain's line, not a model. And every later polygamous household in the canon is shown breeding exactly the misery you would expect: Sarah and Hagar, Leah and Rachel, Hannah and Peninnah, Solomon's wives turning away his heart. The standard was fixed before any of it: “Therefore shall a man leave his father and his mother, and shall cleave unto his wife: and they shall be one flesh” (Gen 2:24).

The larger corruption is the claim that marriage is a social construction which each age may redefine. The Lord Jesus settled the question by going back past Moses to the beginning: “Have ye not read, that he which made them at the beginning made them male and female, And said, For this cause shall a man leave father and mother, and shall cleave to his wife: and they twain shall be one flesh?” (Mat 19:4-5). Two sexes, one man, one woman, one flesh, joined by God. Everything else — Lamech's two wives, Esau's Canaanite marriages, and every modern redefinition offered since — is measured against that and found to be departure. Esau's marriages were “a grief of mind unto Isaac and to Rebekah” (Gen 26:35), and Scripture expects the reader to feel the same grief.

Greek & Hebrew Roots

Hebrew 'Adah (H5711), Adah, ornament; 'adah (H5710), to deck, adorn; 'ishshah (H802), woman, wife; dabaq (H1692), to cleave; basar 'echad, one flesh.

expand to see more

Hebrew 'Adah (H5711) — Adah; ornament, adornment; borne by two women in Genesis.

Hebrew 'adah (H5710) — to pass on, to deck or adorn oneself; the root of the name.

Hebrew 'ishshah (H802) — woman, wife; the word of Gen 2:24 and of Lamech's two.

Hebrew dabaq (H1692) — to cling, cleave, be joined fast; the verb of the marriage ordinance.

Hebrew morath ruach — bitterness of spirit; Gen 26:35's “grief of mind” at Esau's wives.

Usage

"“Lamech took unto him two wives” — the first departure from the one-flesh pattern."

"“Adah bare Jabal” — culture and violence growing on the same branch."

"“Adah the daughter of Elon the Hittite” — a marriage that grieved a covenant household."
